title: Contextual Degradation Logbook
content:
Purpose: capture informal, iterative notes about prompt-level and few-shot-level behaviors that systematically degrade as conversation/context length increases. Focus is desktop experiments (hosted API) and local quantized runner runs. Goal: distill reproducible failures and simple mitigations (template transforms, shot ordering, prefix caching heuristics).

High-level hypothesis:
- Many prompt patterns that 'work' at short context lengths (<= 1k tokens) break when earlier context moves out of the active KV cache or when the model must rely on weaker retrieval.
- Failures cluster into three types: 1) reference loss (model forgets or misattributes earlier facts), 2) instruction drift (tone/formatting changes mid-response), 3) hallucinated constraints (model fabricates constraints or denies earlier explicit instructions).

Quick experiment matrix (notes):
- Model: gpt-open-1.2b-quant (local), redwood-host/g-small (hosted)
- Config vars varied: sequence length (512 / 1024 / 2048), fewshot size (0/1/3/8), shot order (canonical -> reverse), system prompt presence (yes/no), temperature (0.0 / 0.2 / 0.7), prefix cache enabled (on/off)
- Observed metric: failure_rate (manual triage), disagreement_count (token-level inconsistent references), latency impact (ms), token cost (hosted).

Notable micro-experiments and outcomes:
1) Few-shot anchor ordering (3-shot)
   - Template A: canonical ordering (ex1, ex2, ex3) placed directly before query
   - Template B: shuffled ordering each request (ex3, ex1, ex2)
   - Result: canonical ordering reduced 'format drift' but increased sensitivity to exact phrasing in examples. Shuffled yielded more stable correctness on longer contexts (>= 1500 tokens) — hypothesis: shuffling forces model to rely on pattern induction over position-dependent cues.

2) System prompt as remote reference vs inlined facts
   - Inline facts (duplicated in prompt body) reduce reference loss but raise token cost and latency; for long sessions, duplication is unsustainable.
   - Remote system (attached only once at session start) saves tokens but when remote anchor ages out of KV cache, the model begins to contradict prior facts.
   - Partial mitigation: include a 1-2 sentence dynamic recap in each user message (cheap but effective).

3) Prefix-cache stress test
   - With prefix caching enabled, repeating introduction tokens reduced compute for bursts, but when we switched to different user personas mid-session, cache mismatch amplified instruction drift.
   - Note: add logic to invalidate cache on persona-switch events.

Representative few-shot set (3-shot) used in multiple tests:
- EX1: "Task: Convert the following requirements into a bulleted checklist. Input: 

"Make login email optional; add MFA; log IP on failure."
  Output: 
  - Make email input optional
  - Require MFA for admin accounts
  - Log failed login IP with timestamp

- EX2: "Task: Convert the following into a checklist. Input:

"Turn off feature-flag X during migration; notify team."
  Output: 
  - Disable feature-flag X during DB migration
  - Notify SRE and Product channels

- EX3: "Task: Convert into checklist. Input:

"Archive old user data after 180 days; keep consent logs."
  Output: 
  - Archive user data older than 180 days
  - Retain consent logs for compliance

Observed failure: when adding ~1200 tokens of prior chat history before this few-shot block, model occasionally omits the explicit 'retain consent logs' item and invents a new bullet about 'run monthly audits' (hallucination).

Failure case catalog (examples to reproduce) — short reproducible prompts: 
- Case A (reference loss): provide a 400-token user story, then a 1300-token conversation, then ask a direct question about the early user story. Expected: answer refers to the original user story. Actual: model claims details differ.
- Case B (instruction drift): start with strict output format (JSON with fields a,b,c). After three turns and many examples, model outputs freeform text.
- Case C (hallucinated constraints): prompt says 'do not assume budget > $0'. Later model replies: 'Given the budget of $500...'

Notes on debugging approach: 
- Re-run failed prompts at 3 different seed temps (0/0.2/0.7) to see if deterministic decoding reduces hallucinations.
- Reorder/concatenate few-shot exemplars; test 'indicator tokens' (“BEGIN_EXAMPLE” / “END_EXAMPLE”) to make boundaries explicit.
- Try compressed recap: before query, insert a 2-3 sentence recap created by a deterministic summarizer chain (cheap LM call) — often rescues reference loss with small token overhead.

Practical heuristics that looked promising (notes-to-self):
- Keep critical invariant statements (e.g., compliance constraints) in a tiny immutable prefix repeated every N user messages. Empirical N ~ 5 for 1.2B models; larger models can tolerate more.
- For long sessions, use rolling summaries: every K tokens create a 1-2 sentence recap and append to prompt; eject older recaps. Works better than re-including full text.
- For few-shot examples, prefer conceptual variety over lexical similarity; diverse phrasing reduces brittle matching.
- Add explicit 'ignore earlier hallucinations' instruction following any system update to force the model to re-evaluate.
